This person is a 28-year-old Sudanese asylum seeker currently in Calais who used to teach secondary school science; he cares about the policy introducing humanitarian visas issued by UK consulates in France and Belgium, expanding family reunion eligibility beyond spouses/children to include dependent siblings, and a 30-day target for initial screening interviews by secure video so he can travel safely rather than risk a small-boat crossing, because his younger sister lives in Birmingham and he has already been extorted by smugglers. This person is a 47-year-old local authority housing director in the North East of England; she cares about replacing hotel use with a dispersal scheme that caps placements per ward, front-loads per-person integration grants to councils, allows councils to procure modular housing with capital support, and requires 12-week advance data on arrivals (age, school needs), because she must plan school places and homelessness budgets responsibly. This person is a 39-year-old care home operator in Greater Manchester employing 120 staff; she cares about allowing asylum seekers to work in shortage-occupation roles after three months, rapid right-to-work verification through the Home Office Employer Checking Service, funded ESOL classes aligned to care certificates, and portability of DBS checks, because chronic vacancies are closing beds and residents are waiting for care. This person is a 45-year-old trade union organiser for social care workers in Birmingham; he cares that any right-to-work reform includes proactive enforcement by the labour market inspectorate, bans on tied employer accommodation, guaranteed access to unions in asylum accommodation, and whistleblower protections with fast status regularisation for exploited workers, because he has documented wage theft and unsafe conditions in the sector. This person is a 50-year-old NHS trust operations manager in East Kent; she cares about a funded protocol requiring initial health assessments within 72 hours of arrival, ring-fenced tariffs for vaccination catch-up, TB screening and mental health triage with interpreters, and data-sharing agreements so booking into GP lists doesn’t affect immigration decisions, because A&E gets overwhelmed when people arrive without primary care registration. This person is a 33-year-old faith leader in Glasgow who coordinates a community sponsorship group; he cares about expanding sponsorship quotas, standardised training and safeguarding checks for sponsors, a modest per-capita integration grant to cover housing deposits and ESOL, and a clear pathway from temporary protection to indefinite leave after five years, because his congregation has successfully hosted families but struggles without predictable support. This person is a 45-year-old Home Office asylum operations manager in London who wants a clear, published service standard (e.g., initial decisions within 6 months) backed by a triage model that fast-tracks manifestly well-founded claims, consolidates interviews into a single trauma‑informed session with accredited interpreters, uses secure digital document upload to cut missing-paper delays, and limits late evidence without good cause; they care because backlog KPIs, staff burnout, and hotel costs are spiraling under the current fragmented process. This person is a 38-year-old immigration solicitor in Manchester funded through legal aid who opposes offshoring and inadmissibility rules that block claims, and argues for guaranteed access to counsel before substantive interviews, extended appeal deadlines for trauma survivors, publicly available country guidance disclosure, and an independent oversight panel to audit interview quality; they care because they’ve seen clients unlawfully refused due to rushed fast-track procedures and inadequate interpretation. This person is a 56-year-old leader of a district council in Kent who supports ending the use of commercial hotels via a statutory dispersal formula that caps placements by GP panel size and school places, requires 8 weeks’ notice before new accommodation opens, and guarantees ring-fenced per-capita funding paid quarterly in advance; they care because unmanaged placements have blown their temporary housing budget and strained local services without predictable reimbursement. This person is a 32-year-old HM Treasury analyst in London who backs a costed reform package that hires more caseworkers on permanent contracts, replaces hotels with time-limited leases on empty MOD and university stock, allows work after 6 months to reduce Section 95 support, and publishes a whole‑of‑government fiscal scorecard; they care because modelling shows that spending on casework capacity and work rights yields net savings versus prolonged accommodation and litigation. This person is a 35-year-old CTO of a GovTech firm in Edinburgh proposing a secure case management platform with multilingual portals for applicants and counsel, automated interview scheduling, eIDV with on‑device biometrics, and open APIs for councils and NGOs to coordinate housing and health referrals; they care because their pilots with local authorities show digital intake can cut no‑show rates and reduce processing times by months. This person is a 29-year-old privacy and civil liberties advocate in Cardiff who insists any digitisation include statutory data minimisation, independent algorithmic audits, bans on live facial recognition at intake, strict deletion schedules for biometrics once status is decided, and an explicit prohibition on data sharing with origin‑country governments; they care because undocumented people avoid services when they fear surveillance, undermining both fairness and system accuracy.
